title: The 5 Fragrance Trends Set To Define Fall, According To A Master Perfumer
text:
The 5 Fragrance Trends Set To Define Fall, According To A Master Perfumer

If the name Alberto Morillas doesn’t immediately ring a bell, the names on his impressive CV certainly might. Calvin Klein CK One, Gucci Bloom, Marc Jacobs Daisy, Flower by Kenzo — these are perfumes we’ve all encountered in one way or another, whether they’ve taken pride of place on your own perfume shelf, remind you of a loved one’s signature scent, or inspired a fleeting spritz at the department store, hoping you’d come back one day and finally make the purchase. Morillas created them all.

In other words, what Morillas — now the founder of his own perfume brand, Mizensir — doesn’t know about perfume probably isn’t worth knowing. Which makes him particularly well placed to predict the biggest and most interesting fragrance trends for the seasons ahead. And what’s that? A slight chill in the air? Whether you’re hankering for pumpkin spice or hanging on to the last days of sunshine, fall is right around the corner, and with it comes a whole new laundry list of notes, accords, and ways to wear your fragrance.

Ahead, Morillas predicts the top perfume trends to watch this fall, and how to make them work for you.

DashDividers_1_500x100

Bitter & Dark Notes

Gourmand fragrances — perfumes with edible, dessert-like notes — are everywhere you turn, but Morillas predicts that this fall, we’ll have had our fill of strawberries, caramel, and Chantilly cream. “These notes are quite simple,” Morillas says, “but a perfume with true depth features a slight bitterness to it.” This is why fragrance brands are leaning towards slightly more unusual notes. “Think artichoke, herbs like thyme, grass such as vetiver, and plants like cypriol,” says Morillas — all of which add a herbaceous, mysterious edge to counteract the saccharine sweetness of popular notes like vanilla.

Creed’s Wild Vetiver Eau de Parfum boasts grassy vetiver and zingy pink pepper to balance the lush rose and syrupy berries. Then there’s Mizensir Mythique Vetyver, with vetiver, Sicilian lemon, and geranium bourbon — a leafy, green rose. If you have less to spend, try Le Monde Gourmand Santal Supreme, with green vetiver, skin-like musk, and sweet, powdery violet.

Pre-Scenting Your Clothes

Having a perfume base layer — like using a scented body wash or body lotion — before applying fragrance is nothing new, and can help you smell better for longer. But Morillas thinks most of these products smell pretty ordinary. If you’ve found a perfume you really love and want to maximize its sillage — the scent cloud that follows you around all day — Morillas recommends scenting your wardrobe.

It’s as simple as investing in a porcelain or ceramic hanging ornament, spritzing your favorite fragrance all over it, then placing it inside your wardrobe so the scent molecules gradually infuse the fabric of your clothes, enhancing your overall scent. It pays to choose fragrances with excellent staying power, anyway. I love Mizensir Ylang Spirit, with warm, solar notes of jasmine, vanilla, and bergamot. Also try R29 Fragrance Award 2026 winners: Diptyque Orphéon Eau de Parfum, with gin-like juniper berries and vanilla-esque tonka bean, and Byredo Future Memories Eau de Parfum, a smorgasbord of clean orange blossom, rich vanilla liquor accord, and tart blackcurrant.

If you really want to infuse your threads, opt for an extrait de parfum — one of the highest fragrance concentrations.

Burnt Notes

Bonfires? In fall? Groundbreaking. But smoky woods, charred cedar, and a hint of burnt embers are pretty revolutionary in fragrance, according to Morillas, who predicts that the creamy, green woods we know and love in fragrances like Phlur’s Father Figure and Refinery29 Fragrance Award 2026 winner Maya Njie Nordic Cedar are taking on a toasted effect this season.

“Fire notes are not easy to capture because there’s so much nuance,” says Morillas. “Smoke, burning embers, and ash all have different smells,” he continues, “but they’re perfect for fall because they’re so cocooning.” There’s also a danger element to them, adds Morillas, which makes them exciting.

AllSaints Naked Woods opens with verdant notes of tart apple and freshly picked rhubarb — green leaves and all — but dries down to something warm and cozy thanks to amber woods, which smell richer and darker than green, creamy woods like cedar. Also try Kilian Paris Midnight Espresso Eau de Parfum, with coffee, hazelnut, and rum, which lend a roasted edge, and Cyklar Amber Hour, a combination of amber resin, singed palo santo, and vanilla-like tonka bean.

The Apothecary Effect

Basil, fresh herbs, and minty notes are making their way into fragrance, bringing the same easy appeal they have in food, says Morillas. He describes them as “simple pleasures” in both taste and scent: fresh, uplifting and familiar. Just as a handful of herbs can transform a simple dish, they can give a fragrance an instant lift, adding a hit of freshness and vibrancy — a welcome antidote to fall and winter’s greying skies.

Mizensir’s Anticonformiste Eau de Parfum is minty, zesty, and woody in equal measure, making it our top pick here. Also try Olfactory X Mint + Apricot Eau de Parfum, with basil and mint alongside sun-warmed apricot, tangy blackcurrant, and syrupy dates. We also love Uni’s Sunset Water-Based Perfume, an aromatic mix of crushed mint and zingy lemon with grassy patchouli and smoked sandalwood. Then there’s ‘Ôrəbella WINDOW2SOUL Parfum, where fresh mint slices through heady damask rose and jasmine.

Cool Musks

The musk perfumes we all know and love have a distinct skin-like quality to them, reminiscent of stepping out of a warm bath or pulling on a loved one’s well-worn sweater. But there’s a new musk in town, says Morillas — and instead of skin, it smells like the great outdoors: crisp air, cool greenery, and freshly cut grass.

“I call these ‘cool’ musks,” says Morillas. “It’s hard to capture the sensation of coolness,” he adds, “but we do this by including one particular note: camphor.” A waxy substance derived from the camphor laurel tree, camphor is often used in chest rubs thanks to its medicinal, cooling, and invigorating qualities — which, in fragrance, translates to that elusive sensation of icy coolness.

There’s a dash of this in Ellis Brooklyn’s DEAR SKY Eau de Parfum (think pink pepper, honeydew melon, and zippy bergamot), Yves Saint Laurent Libre Berry Crush Eau de Parfum (creamy coconut, soothing lavender, and juicy raspberry), and Givenchy Very Irresistible Eau de Parfum (spicy star anise, sprightly blackberry, and buttery vanilla).

Scenting Your… Hands

Lastly, your hands are one of the most underrated places to wear fragrance, hints Morillas. Think scented hand sanitizer or a fragrant hand cream, then bring the scent up over your wrists and onto the backs of your hands. It makes sense. We use our hands constantly — typing at our keyboards, reaching for our phones, running our fingers through our hair — so every movement creates a little burst of fragrance. It’s also one of the easiest ways to enjoy your own perfume throughout the day, rather than leaving an obvious scent trail for everyone else.

No one does scented hand cream better than Cyklar. Try Sacred Santal, which smells like an enchanted woodland while packing urea and ectoin — two seriously moisturizing ingredients that help keep hands soft and smooth. Then there’s Salt & Stone’s Bergamot & Hinoki Nourishing Hand Cream, formulated with hydrating niacinamide and softening seaweed extract. And one of our favorites, which needs no introduction: Glossier You Hand Cream.

title: What I Think About When I Choose How I Smell As A Trans Woman
text:
What I Think About When I Choose How I Smell As A Trans Woman

Welcome to Note to Self, Refinery29’s fragrance series exploring perfume beyond the bottle. Through intimate stories and scent memories, we’re unpacking the emotions, experiences, and identities behind the fragrances we wear — and why they can become such a deeply meaningful part of who we are.

What’s in a name? That which we call a rose by any other name would smell as sweet.”

When I came out as trans in 2017, this well-known Shakespeare line held a lot of meaning as I chose my name. Overlooked by so many, our names are an important part of our identity, and as a trans woman, hearing people use mine — like external acceptance of my authentic self — was incredibly affirming. But in hindsight, I missed something important in that quote: the sense of smell.

You see, the fragrances we choose are just as integral to our identities as our monikers. Patchouli, ylang-ylang, cedar, and so many other names belonging to notes of a different type from the ones I recognized as a musician now jumped out at me as I found ways to express myself.

Before I came out, the fragrances I bought were as gender neutral as possible. It was my way of avoiding masculinity and being able to secretly embrace who I really was. After coming out, an entirely different world was unlocked, and I quickly realized that changing my fragrance was just as exciting, not to mention cathartic, as updating my wardrobe.

I was on a mission to find my style and a scent that encapsulated that. Was I sweet? Perhaps floral? Or was I something bolder? The first fragrance I bought was Katy Perry’s Mad Love, sadly now discontinued. It was a light, fruity, and playful fragrance that allowed me to express my femininity in a fun way, at a time in my life when I was finding ways to show up in the world — even if that did involve some questionable outfit choices. Most importantly, it was affordable. As a trans woman, I was condensing years of “growing up” into months, on top of everyday adult life. While the cis women I knew were able to experiment and refine their style in their younger years, I was on an Instagram-fueled crash course in makeup and style; I wasn’t ready to splash out on fine fragrance just yet.

As it turns out, I wasn’t the only one who felt a need to balance cost with an existing connection. Journalist Sophie Layton, 23, tells me, “My first fragrance was a SO…? body spray; I think it was Wild Berries. I had decided I wanted to start with that brand because it was one that my best friend (and basically big sister) used herself, and she played such an important role in my transition, especially in the early days.” It was a good balance of fun but not bank-breaking, says Layton.

After coming out, Summer Healey, 37, regularly jumped at any offers of perfume samples to discover and experiment with notes she liked before settling on Prada Paradoxe Eau de Parfum — a heady bouquet of neroli, jasmine, and orange blossom. “I remember Prada being a brand I always resonated with visually, but smelling that first Paradoxe sample, I was hooked by the soft floral tones that felt like an inner home,” she recalls. Healey continues, “Early transition — even before being out socially — having my scent felt like wearing armour, and smelling it on my wrists made me feel more confident.”

In a society that demonizes us more than it tries to understand us, confidence is everything when taking those steps outside. After all, we go to work, we meet friends, and we walk our dogs just like everyone else, but with an added layer of caution. Even as someone who’s been out for nine years, I’m always looking over my shoulder when I’m out in public, always ready for abuse — or to run. It’s no surprise that how we express ourselves is also influenced by a need for safety. For me, it’s how I present and how I smell, hoping that if a passerby catches the scent of my fragrance, they don’t stop to question who just walked past. It seems Layton agrees: “Being seen to put on body spray definitely helps [with the] perception of others,” she tells me.

On my journey of expression, it’s not just my transness that I’ve learned a lot about. As someone diagnosed with autism and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (AuDHD), I’ve discovered my sense of smell has been an unwitting co-pilot in my transness and self-expression all along. A smell is either awful and offensive, or it’s amazing and stimulates my brain. There’s no in-between, just full-on intensity. The result has been curating a careful balance of expressive scents that will also help ground me and regulate my mood and emotions.

My latest go-to fragrances are Versace Dylan Purple Eau de Parfum (think juicy pear, effervescent bergamot, and Iso E Super — a molecule that smells different on everyone), and YSL Black Opium Eau de Parfum (with sweet vanilla, bitter coffee, and airy orange blossom). Both are sweet and joyful but with more distinct, confident notes and more immediate presence. Since my first Katy Perry fragrance, a lot has changed. I’ve grown up, and these fragrances are the latest bookmark in my current chapter of life.

But here’s the thing: I can’t ignore how heavily gendered fragrances can be. We’re practically told what we can or can’t buy, and it’s all in the language brands use to market them. “Daisy, by Marc Jacobs. The fragrance for women” or “Boss Bottled. The Man of Today.” But why can’t men wear sweet, floral fragrances? The answer lies in the same box as why a man wouldn’t dream of ordering a cheeky glass of rosé when on a night out with the boys.

In unpacking my own identity, I was also unpacking the box of gender constructs. Historically, men were perceived as tough and strong, while women were delicate and nurturing, giving rise to the modern stereotypes that hold us back today. Despite concerted attempts as a society to leave these stereotypes behind, the fragrance industry still relies on gendered cues to appeal to us for one simple reason: consumerism. Douglas Little, CEO and founder of Heretic Parfum, a brand that has been pushing the boundaries and perceptions of fragrance, tells me, “For centuries, perfume wasn’t divided into ‘for him’ and ‘for her.’ Scent was ritual, medicine, seduction, power, status.” Take ancient Egypt, where fragrant oils were used in religious practices as well as worn for beauty across genders. Similarly, in ancient Rome, fragrance was often a marker of wealth and social standing.

Little adds, “The idea that a rose belongs to women or leather belongs to men is a remarkably modern invention, one born less from art than from marketing. Once fragrance became a mass-market commodity, it became easier to sell if everything was neatly divided into two aisles.” The irony, says Little, is that scent has no gender: “Vetiver doesn’t know who is wearing it; jasmine isn’t feminine; oud isn’t masculine. These are stories we’ve assigned to raw materials, and after hearing them long enough, we’ve mistaken them for truth.”

But to a certain extent, trans people do embrace gendered cues, and not just for protection. Layton says, “For a lot of people, they’ve spent a significant chunk of their lives being told, ‘You can’t do x, wear y, or use z, because it’s for girls’, so when they come out, doing all of those things that can be considerably feminizing [like] reclaiming that in a way.”

Trans advocate Robyn Newark, 39, tells me, “I’ve had past experiences of hating masculine scented products like shower gel and shaving cream, so changing those to feminine ones feels more affirming and freeing, especially when you’ve previously felt like you exist in a prison of expected gender presentation — including scent.” Certainly, clothing or the length of my hair is an obvious form of outward expression, but I feel it’s more symbolic and doesn’t fully capture just how incredibly personal that reclamation process is.

Personally, fragrance is the key — a feeling that can be applied to any outfit, giving it depth and meaning. “To me, wearing perfume is one of the most intimate acts of self-expression we have,” says Little. “It’s invisible, deeply personal, and impossible to fully explain.” Little adds, “The most heretical thing we can do isn’t create another fragrance; it’s freeing people from the idea that scent needs permission to belong to them.” A fragrance can not only add something to our outfits and to how we feel, but it can also lend itself to moments, too. “Smell is definitely a little bit more for me than for anyone else,” says Newark. “I also enjoy it when engaging in intimate play with others, sometimes choosing to spritz my lower back or lower stomach.”

While fragrance is likely to remain gendered for quite some time, our love/hate relationship with it needn’t be so toxic. After all, it’s easier to find your identity when you know who you’re not, or what you don’t like, right? What some see as preference, I see as meaning. Gendered cues are simply my starting point; non-statutory guidance that I can choose to embrace, or not. Little agrees: “I’ve always believed fragrance should express who you are, not who society expects you to be. At Heretic, we don’t compose perfumes around gender; we compose around emotion, atmosphere and desire. I want someone to choose a fragrance because it makes them feel haunted, dangerous, euphoric, nostalgic, or transformed, not because it was placed on the ‘correct’ shelf.”

As I look at my shelf and the fragrance collection I’ve accumulated over the last nine years, I see far more than something that completes an outfit. Curated by my neurodiversity and my trans identity, I see a timeline. A visual and deeply personal representation of how far I’ve come, with each one unlocking intimate emotions and core memories of my self-discovery. Every spray is a part of my journey that I choose to share with others, all while reminding myself that we are not static beings, but individuals who can redefine boundaries as we continue to grow.

title: I Own Over 300 Perfumes, But These 7 Earn Me The Most Compliments
text:
I Own Over 300 Perfumes, But These 7 Earn Me The Most Compliments

Welcome to Note to Self, Refinery29’s fragrance series exploring perfume beyond the bottle. Through intimate stories and scent memories, we’re unpacking the emotions, experiences, and identities behind the fragrances we wear — and why they can become such a deeply meaningful part of who we are.

If I had to hazard a guess, I’d say I own more than 300 fragrances. As a perfume content creator and certified fragrance specialist, scent is my entire job — and I don’t discriminate. My collection spans everything from niche houses like Ex Nihilo and Initio Parfums to budget-friendly gems (Zara’s fragrances, created in collaboration with Jo Malone, are seriously underrated).

While I have plenty of long-time favorites that I return to despite the constant stream of new launches, only a select few consistently stop people in their tracks. If you ask me, there’s no better feeling than someone complimenting your perfume. It validates your personal taste and leaves a lasting impression long after you’ve left the room.

With that in mind, I wanted to share the handful of fragrances that never fail to turn heads. Whether you’re looking for a new signature scent or want a perfume that people can’t help but ask about, these are the bottles that have proven themselves time and time again — and I’m willing to bet they’ll do the same for you.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Eudora Nwasike (@a.dose.of.e)

DashDividers_1_500x100

Giorgio Armani Stronger With You Powerfully Eau de Parfum

Just when you thought the Stronger With You line couldn’t get any better, Armani dropped its best flanker yet. Stronger With You Powerfully gave me a literal nosegasm. It’s an addictive blend of juicy cherry, smoked chestnut, and rich bourbon vanilla that still stays true to the collection’s signature DNA of warm, smoky vanilla and fresh, herbaceous lavender. If you’re looking for a first-date fragrance that’ll have them leaning in and asking, “What are you wearing?”, this right here is the one.

Zara Fashionably London Elixir Parfum

Out of every fragrance in Zara’s Cities collection — created by Jo Malone CBE, no less — Fashionably London Elixir is the one I keep coming back to. It’s a sweet, airy rose, but nothing like the old-school, powdery florals you might be imagining. Instead, sparkling bergamot and clean, skin-like musk give it a fresh, modern edge. It smells effortlessly sophisticated and, on me, lasts more than eight hours on both skin and clothes. Talk about bang for your buck. If you’re after a bougie-on-a-budget fragrance that’ll work for literally any occasion, any time of year, start here.

Amouage Purpose Eau de Parfum

Amouage Purpose is a modern classic and one that will always have a place in my ever-growing collection. It’s a spicy, smoky, woody fragrance built around frankincense, pimento (yes, the pepper!), sandalwood, and akigalawood, a sustainable molecule derived from patchouli. Whenever I wear it, it never fails to attract compliments. I’m talking, “Wow, you smell unreal,” or “I could smell you before I saw you — I need to know what perfume you’re wearing.” It’s a true projection monster, so a little goes a very long way. The fact that it gets people talking comes as no surprise, since the brand recently took home two wins at the 2026 Fragrance Foundation Awards.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Eudora Nwasike (@a.dose.of.e)

Balmain Carbone Eau de Parfum

Balmain Carbone was composed by one of the most prolific perfumers of our time, Quentin Bisch (think Carolina Herrera Good Girl, Chloé Nomade, and Parfums de Marly Delina), yet it feels incredibly special and unique. If you like fragrances in the realm of Amouage Guidance (creamy, spicy and rich — like an indulgent dessert), Carbone will be right up your street. It’s a beautiful composition of musky suede rose with woody touches that give it a more androgynous edge. Four to six spritzes and the compliments will be rolling in all day.

Phlur Cherry Stem Eau de Parfum

Phlur’s Cherry Stem may not be the most talked-about fragrance in the collection, but if you ask me, it’s seriously underrated. Juicy black cherry meets soft leather and warm caramel, while a subtle boozy edge keeps it from becoming tooth-achingly saccharine. It’s sweet without being sticky, with moderate projection that means you’ll catch those addictive little wafts throughout the day (or night). If you’re new to fragrance or want something that feels effortless and cool without trying too hard, Cherry Stem is the perfect place to start.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Eudora Nwasike (@a.dose.of.e)

Byredo Bal d’Afrique Absolu de Parfum

When I smell this, it instantly transports me to the Caribbean — and I think that’s exactly why people comment on it so much. Who doesn’t want to feel like they’re on vacation every day? Bright bergamot and tart blackcurrant open the fragrance before melting into a delectable praline note, followed by a warm, woody, amber base. Despite the deeper notes, it remains clean, airy, and fresh. I love layering it with Maison Francis Kurkdjian Baccarat Rouge 540 Extrait to amplify the praline’s addictive sweetness.

Frédéric Malle Contre-Jour Eau de Parfum

Contre-Jour may have only launched this year, but it’s already become one of my most complimented fragrances. It was love at first sniff and showcases the beauty and complexity of immortelle, the everlasting flower, in all its honeyed, smoky glory. A generous dose of rose creates a stunning contrast, while soft sandalwood with a subtle herbal edge keeps the composition feeling natural and refined. It’s the kind of fragrance that makes people stop and ask what I’m wearing — not because it announces itself, but because it leaves behind a trail that feels expensive. If I had to describe it in three words, they’d be artistic, complex, and enigmatic. This is a scent for those who appreciate the finer things in life.
